extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of comparative religion and mythology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological guidance for interpreting myths and studying comparative religion, summarizing competing schools (philological, anthropological, ritualist) and practical tests for evaluating mythic explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language's role / verbal vs material myth
rubrics_metrics.description: Language has had a great share in the formation of myth; descriptive names become personal and verbal metaphor can expand into myth. Material myth (based on real and sensible analogy) is primary and verbal myth secondary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish as far as possible myth founded on fact (material myth) from myth founded on word (verbal myth). Beware that verbal metaphor has an essential weakness and that language both follows imagination and independently produces mythic conceptions ('a disease of language').

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathy with the untutored mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The student of myth must possess the ability to transport himself into the imaginative atmosphere of the untutored mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the cognitive stance of the people whose myths you study to see how natural phenomena could be construed as personal or divine; this imaginative sympathy is essential for plausible reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious use of circumstantial analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: In interpreting heroic legend as based on nature-myth, circumstantial analogy must be very cautiously appealed to and there is need of evidence more cogent than vague likenesses between human and cosmic life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept superficial resemblances as proof; seek corroborating cases where myths openly figure familiar aspects of nature, and prefer examples where etymology or explicit naming confirms natural referents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etymology as guide and safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: The etymology of names is at once the guide and safeguard of the mythologist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use etymological analysis to recover earlier meanings (e.g., Helios = sun), but treat philological conclusions cautiously and cross-check with other evidence because etymologies can be misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider allegory but do not overemphasize it
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegory cannot maintain the large place often claimed for it, yet it cannot be passed over by the mythologist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize allegorical myths (e.g., Pandora, Herakles choosing) but avoid explaining all myths as allegory; weigh the plausibility of allegorical readings against other lines of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity of development — myth as organic product
rubrics_metrics.description: Legend, when classified on a sufficient scale, displays a regularity of development which must be attributed to laws of formation; it becomes possible to treat myth as an organic product of mankind at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for systematic patterns and developmental regularities across traditions that suggest lawful formation processes rather than pure fancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of myth to history — myths as historical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the search for mutilated traditions of real events may be difficult, myth-shapers have preserved masses of sound historical evidence unconsciously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss potential historical cores in myths; investigate whether myths may encode memories of real events, but require careful corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animistic explanation for spirit belief (Tylor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Animistic theory: man first attained to the idea of spirit by reflection on sleep, dreams, trances, shadows, hallucinations, breath, and death, and gradually peopled nature with spirits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining origins of spirit-belief, consider experiential bases (sleep, dreams, etc.) as plausible generators of animistic ideas; apply this as one theoretical model among others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize ritual over myth in ancient religion study
rubrics_metrics.description: In the study of ancient religions we must begin, not with myth, but with ritual and traditional usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat myth often as an explanation of ritual rather than its origin; examine rites and practices first because ritual tends to be fixed while myth is variable and explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth as explanation of ritual; regard myth as variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths connected with sanctuaries and ceremonies are usually explanations of religious usages; ritual was fixed and myth variable, arising often when original sense of usage had been lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a myth clusters around a ritual, consider the likelihood that the ritual is primary and the myth secondary—seek the original functional context for the rite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal/natural sense of myths as testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancient myths, taken in their natural sense, without allegorical gloss, are of great importance as testimonies to the prevalent views of the gods when they were formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor natural/surface readings of myths as direct testimonies to belief and conceptions of deity, while remaining open to symbolic or allegorical layers when justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservatism and sacredness indicated by transmission stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Children's dislike of alteration in folk-tale suggests a conservatism that may be a legacy of religious dread of tampering with tales of the gods; the religious story is tribal property and central to faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use patterns of transmission and resistance to alteration (e.g., in children's receptions) as indirect evidence for the sacredness and stability of particular myths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropological method: study myths in their rudest shape
rubrics_metrics.description: The anthropological method enables us to explain many phenomena by studying myths in their rudest and most primitive shape and reveals survivals of earlier barbaric ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare myths across widely different cultures, emphasize primitive forms and social contexts (totemism, magic), and look for survivals and parallels rather than relying solely on philological etymologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of the anthropological method; avoid exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The anthropological school 'cannot answer all the questions which the science of mythology must solve' and may be 'too exclusive' with ignorant camp-followers seeing totems and fetishes everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply anthropological explanations as the sole account; remain critical of overgeneralization and cross-check anthropological inferences with philology, ritual studies, and historical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish religious vs mythical moods but expect overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between the religious mood (earnest contemplation) and the mythical mood (playful and erratic fancy), but a hard and fast line cannot be drawn between myth and religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying material, recognize degrees between sacred religious tradition and playful mythic material; examine audience, context (initiated vs general), and function within society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek intellectual-historical conditions for myth origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to find an historical condition of the human intellect to which the element in myths regarded as irrational shall seem rational enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain irrational features of myths by reconstructing mental habits, knowledge levels, and cognitive states of the periods/peoples in which myths originated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze developmental stages of myths (savage, civilized, popular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Much ancient myth is composed of (1) the savage 'explanation', (2) the civilized and poetic modification of it, and (3) the later popular idea of the original tale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically parse myths into possible stages of development, tracing survivals from earlier stages and later literary or popular embellishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of undesigned coincidence (recurrence) for mythic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Tylor's (and Lang's) 'test of undesigned coincidence' (the test of recurrence) serves as a criterion of the value of myth—independent recurrence across cultures strengthens a mythic interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use undesigned coincidences (recurring elements in independent traditions) as supportive evidence for interpretations, while still considering alternative explanations like diffusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution with philological etymologies; verify scholarly logic
rubrics_metrics.description: The philological method is inadequate and misleading for discovering the origin of a myth or physical explanation of the oldest myths; it is especially difficult to conjecture the meaning of proper, local, and mythical names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat bold etymological equations skeptically; check etymologies against other disciplines and seek consensus among specialists before adopting linguistic explanations as decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain diffusion case-by-case: universal mental habits vs borrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: The diffusion of identical myths may be due to universal prevalence of similar mental habits or to borrowing/transmission; this argument will scarcely account for world-wide distribution of long and intricate plots and must be checked case-by-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate each apparent parallel on its merits: consider independent invention (mental habits), historical contact and borrowing, and provide evidence for either scenario rather than assuming one explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist overexplanation; require cogent evidence and disciplinary balance
rubrics_metrics.description: It is vain labour to seek a cause for every phenomenon; do not explain every detail by speculative or venturesome ingenuity, and beware of method that 'only glides over questions of the first importance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a cautious, evidence-weighted approach: combine ritual study, philology, ethnography, and historical inquiry; avoid sweeping theories unsupported by diverse corroboration.
